title: Impact of Regional Hydrology on Prairie Pothole Wetlands' Chemistry, Carbon Cycling and Metabolic Balance
content:
ABSTRACT

The Prairie Pothole Region (PPR) in North America is characterized by millions of shallow, marsh and open-water wetlands. These wetlands provide a myriad of ecosystem services, including carbon (C) sequestration, water purification and water storage. Few studies have examined the links between the metabolism and hydrology of PPR wetlands at a landscape scale. Here, we surveyed wetlands across an elevational gradient in the PPR of Alberta, Canada. We combined stable isotope modelling of wetland hydrology, water chemistry and oxygen isotope-derived estimates of metabolic balance. Wetlands at higher elevation had a shorter hydroperiod but were nevertheless more dominated by inflow than their lower elevation, less ephemeral counterparts. While evapoconcentration of salts and C occurred at both high and low elevation, the latter had greater concentrations, possibly due to longer persistence of water on the land and more evaporative influence. Differences in soil type were also linked to wetland inorganic chemistry, but organic matter content was not. Wetland pond metabolic balance (production to respiration ratios) showed no clear connection to hydrology or chemistry, but we found a clear difference between high- (more autotrophic) and low-elevation (more heterotrophic) wetlands. Together, our findings show that regional geography impacts wetland hydrology, with cascading effects on biogeochemical properties and more complex and unresolved links to metabolism.
